div.p: Complex embedded systems are easier to design at a high abstraction level. Synchronous languages have shown to be very adequate for such high-level modeling tasks. In synchronous models, many aspects, time in particular, are handled in a quite abstract fashion, allowing for a design that is not dependent on the target architecture.

Synchronous languages assume that all responses to external stimuli are computed infinitely fast, prior to new arriving external stimuli. It is the task of lower design steps to ensure that timeliness requirements are met even when the actual execution time of the generated code on the target system is taken into account. For this purpose, predicting the execution time of resulting programs (estimating their worst-case execution time, WCET) is necessary. The WCET is the longest possible time a program can execute, i.e. the time it executes, given the worst possible circumstances for a particular set of inputs. In general, WCETs are needed for later real-time scheduling policies and schedulability tests. A schedulability test computes the worst-case response time (WCRT) of a program, which is the longest time taken by the program to complete its computation including possible interferences by other programs, taking a particular scheduling policy into account.

Due to complexity reasons an exact prediction of the WCET/WCRT is computationally intractable for larger systems. Therefore, analysis usually heads for finding an estimate on the WCET/WCRT using an approximation. The result must be both safe as well as accurate, i.e. the value must not be underestimated (to avoid deadline violations) neither should the overestimation be to large to prevent unnecessary waste of resources.

Several advanced timing analysis methods [1,15] and schedulability tests [3,14] have been presented which, however, do not take the complex semantics of any highlevel modeling policy like statecharts into account. That means employing ordinary WCET/WCRT techniques for the analysis of programs generated from statecharts models leads to overestimation. In contrast, exploiting the highlevel semantics of statecharts yields tighter estimates of the WCET/WCRT. This is the main result of this paper.

Following the statecharts semantics, a model starts execution from an initial state, receives signals from the environment and iterates until it reaches a i ¡p Gq r §s Rt state, i.e. until no further action can be triggered without an external signal being sensed. Statecharts models thus react to a stimulus with a chain of actions, where the number of iterations in the chain reaction is not explicitly defined. Therefore, it is an essential feature of our timing analysis method to detect when a stable state is reached. To the authors' knowledge this paper describes the first WCET analysis technique handling synchronous languages, taking into account aspects specific to the semantics of such languages (event concept, states, stability, ...) thus reducing the pessimism on the estimates.
The analysis method presented focuses on the language statecharts and includes the following steps:

1. An annotated control flow graph is generated from each component of the model. For this purpose, the WCETs of the different components are computed. 2. Taking the semantics of statecharts into account, the longest executable path1 in each component of the model is extracted. 3. Finally, using a schedulability test, the worst-case response time of the model is determined. The paper is organized as follows: the next section recapitulates the related work in the field of WCET/WCRT analysis. Section 3 describes the structure and semantics of the statecharts models we consider in this paper. Section 4 introduces the WCET/WCRT analysis technique for synchronous models, and in Section 5 we present some experimental results. Section 6 concludes the paper.

div.p: The WCET of a program can be obtained either measuring the execution times for certain inputs or performing static analysis on the program. Measurement of execution times is usually not feasible since a given system must be tested with all possible input vectors to guarantee the worst-case has also been considered.

Most research on timing analysis is focused on finding an efficient method to determine the WCET of programs. Unfortunately, the problem of static execution time determination is, in the general case, too complex to be solved exactly. Within a reasonable analysis time, only an estimate of the WCET can be determined. Such an estimate must be both § 9 9 § # § R (not too pessimistic) and ¡ 9 (never smaller than the WCET). This is fulfilled by the method presented in this paper.

Much work in the WCET area addresses d fe g §d h i Rj Ck 9j Ci l §m l i n Io 'e o (i.e. on the level of programming languages) and present methods for extracting the longest executable path from programs. The most common approach to this problem is to use annotations to obtain more information about the program from the programmer. User annotations are useful as an aid to automatic analysis, but the goal is to automate the analysis as much as possible since user annotations are error-prone. In our approach user annotations can be used, but are not essential for the analysis, since its main feature is the exploitation of knowledge about the semantics of synchronous languages.

Specific problems encountered at this point are the identification of p )q §r Rs ¡t vu q §w Rx §s [13,1] (Section 4y !z d{ | §} ! } § ) [10] and ) ! § 9 § 9 § R G [5]. Some techniques encountered in automatic program analysis are data flow analysis [2,4,11], abstract interpretation [6] and symbolic execution [7]. Data flow analysis is a standard technique used in compilers to deduce information about dependencies between instructions of a program. Abstract interpretation techniques approximate the semantics of a program language, typically by replacing single values with sets of values. Using symbolic execution, a program is executed using symbolic values for variables instead of concrete values.

In order to calculate execution times, information about the time taken to execute basic blocks2 is also needed. Approaches to the problem of obtaining G § £ R C 9 C timing estimates are mostly concerned with the consideration of pipelining and caching [16,17] and the handling of optimized code [8].

The specification level, where this paper is focused on, is even above high-level. Hence, our method just applies well-known high-and low-level techniques. However, since our method in particular exploits the semantics of synchronous languages, it yields much tighter estimates than ordinary methods could.

Given a model with the WCETs of its different components, the deadlines are checked by a schedulability test [3,14]. A schedulability test computes the WCRT of each component and compares the result to the corresponding deadline. By the time, many accurate as well as approximative schedulability tests have been invented, dedicated to a quite independent set of tasks (with the exception of precedence constraints). However, none of them really covers the complex inter-relationships that can be expressed by the high-level specifications considered in this paper. Taking theses relations into account, as our approach does, an estimate on the WCRT is much more accurate than using ordinary techniques.

An estimate on the WCET of statecharts models could be obtained by compiling the model into C-code and using existing timing analysis methods. However, code generated from high-level models (statecharts models for example) usually consists of many straight-line code blocks related to each other in a quite complicated fashion. For this reason, the result of such a timing analysis would either give a too pessimistic result or it would be very time consuming.

The control flow of high-level programs is hard to recognize in compiled code. It is however much easier to analyze at the level where it has been specified. The control flow of a C-program for example is easier to recognize in the C-program than at the machine-code level.

Most existing timing analyzers for high-level programs analyze the control flow in the high-level program and invoke a low-level timing analyzer, which determine the execution time of basic. Using the control flow and the execution time for the basic blocks, the execution time of the program is then determined.

We present a similar method to determine an upper bound for the WCET of tasks generated from high-level synchronous models. In this case, the control flow is analyzed at the specification level (in the synchronous model). Timing analyzers at the level of high-level programming languages are then invoked to determine the execution times of basic blocks (straight-line code blocks, which can consist of tens or hundreds of lines of code). Our scenario including schedulability analysis is as follows:

1a. An annotated control flow graph (CFG) is generated from the model. For this purpose, the WCET of the code block corresponding to each transition in the model is determined. 1b. By analyzing the trigger of each transition in the statecharts model, all stable states are determined. 2. The WCET is the execution time of the longest executable path. For each path, we also consider events excluding each other in order to detect false paths. Figure 5 shows a path from the stable state S 1 to the stable state S 6 . In the final step, the whole model is analyzed to figure out which Statecharts can be active at the same time. In the Statemate system for example, statements related to the activation or deactivation of components (like "start!", "started", "active" or "stop!") will be considered for this purpose. Groups consisting of concurrent Statecharts are then built.

Given the WCET associated with each node of the CFG and the longest path in the CFG corresponding to each Statechart, the WCRT of each group of Statecharts will be calculated. The WCRT of the model is the maximal WCRT of all groups.

For this purpose, all transitions having a stable state as source are assumed to be executed in the first step (since external events are all sensed only at the beginning of a super step and all events "live" for the duration of one step only). Two of these transitions, t 1 and t 2 , are triggered by external events, while the other transitions (t 3 .. t 5 ) are triggered by local events.

For this purpose, we try to determine whether some transitions, either in parallel states of a Statechart or in concurrent Statecharts, are always executed concurrently.

Given two paths in two parallel states or in two concurrent Statecharts, we first perform a reachability analysis, to check whether the first state on each path can both be active at the same time. If this is the case, we then analyze the labels of the transitions on these paths, and try to find out whether at least two transitions ( 1 and for example) will always be triggered together (in the same step). Dependencies between the triggers and actions associated to the transitions are considered for this purpose.

Note, that if the transitions on two paths in different Statecharts cannot effect each other (their labels contain variables which are all used within a single Statechart), then we assume those two paths to execute concurrently.

The new value for the response time will be compared with the estimated response time for the n o Ep Eq longest combination of paths. If the estimated response time for the next longest combination of paths is still smaller than the execution time of the longest path, the analysis terminates for the corresponding group of Statecharts. Otherwise, the same method will be used to reduce the pessimism on the estimated response time for the next longest combination of paths. This process will be repeated until an estimate on the WCRT has been obtained which cannot be further improved, or a given limit on the computation time has been reached.

In the example of Figure 6, further analysis might yield, that the transition t 3 always follows the transition t 1 and that t 4 and t 5 both always follow t 2 . The new scenario would be therefore as in Figure 7, the super-step containing two steps: 1. the first step, in which t 1 and t 2 are executed and the events triggering t 3 The complexity of the analysis of the triggers depends on the complexity of the triggers and the accuracy of the analysis. The number of possible execution scenarios however grows very fast (exponentially) as the number of considered transitions grows. In fact, there are O(n n ) ways of combining two paths, being the number of transitions on each path. An exhaustive analysis is nevertheless still possible for large models, since statecharts models usually consist of a lot of charts, each, however, containing a relatively small number of transitions.

The WCET/WCRT analysis technique presented in this paper has been implemented as part of a code generator for the STATEMATE system. Some STATEMATE models have been analyzed and the results are presented in Figure 8. In the considered models, the structure of the code sequences associated with the various transitions was simple (this is not a restriction and is quite normal).

For each model, the number of charts, states, transitions, data-items and the WCRT (number of transitions) determined by the analysis are given. For comparison, the longest structural paths are given. These paths were extracted assuming that all Statecharts can be active at the same time and making no difference between external and local events or conditions thus ignoring the statecharts semantics. As shown by Figure 8, exploiting the semantics of statecharts heavily reduces overestimation on WCETs. This is in particular true for larger application examples. After extensively studying the considered models, we can state that in all cases the determined path is identical to the longest executable path to be delivered by an exact method.

In this paper we have presented a method for determining the WCET/WCRT of high-level synchronous models, focusing on the language statecharts. As shown by our experimental results, the new method heavily reduces estimation pessimism due to exploitation of the statecharts semantics. The new method especially includes considerations on how to reach a stable state, of program parts which are mutually exclusive, and on interdependences between various Statecharts. This method has been integrated in a compiler for STATEMATE models within the ESPRIT project 23015 COMITY.
